source.title: High-Dimensional Analysis of Ridge Regression for Non-identically Distributed Data with a Variance Profile
source.authors: Jérémie Bigot; Issa-Mbenard Dabo; C. Male

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes predictive risk across model dimensions in high-dimensional linear regression using random-matrix theory and numerical experiments, rather than the original deep-network settings.
record.gate_note: The paper varies p/n and measures predictive risk for minimum-norm least-squares regression, and varies sample size in the MNIST experiments. Cited results from earlier work are not recorded as rows. Curves without tabulated values are recorded as figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study computes ridgeless (λ=0) predictive risk as p/n varies for linear regression with non-identically distributed features. It uses deterministic equivalents and simulations, a new setting that reports double descent for some variance profiles and triple or quadruple descent for others.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that the quasi doubly stochastic profile reproduces the iid risk formula exactly, and that the optimal ridge λ* is universal across variance profiles. Deterministic equivalents match synthetic data but deviate from real MNIST data, which has correlated features.
record.recipe_differences: This is a random-matrix-theoretic analysis and numerical study of linear ridge/ridgeless regression with variance-profiled data, not a deep-network experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The predictive-risk shape depends on the variance profile; constant and quasi doubly stochastic profiles show double descent, while piecewise constant and block profiles show triple descent and the polynomial profile shows quadruple descent.

fits_no_version.finding: The smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the sample covariance reaches its minimum near p=n for all profiles. Piecewise constant and polynomial profiles show an extended near-zero plateau for p/n in roughly [0.25, 3], which the authors link to multiple descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multiple-descent peaks coincide with extended near-singularity of the empirical covariance spectrum.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal ridge λ*=σ²p/(α²n) minimizes predictive risk for every variance profile, while the GCV-selected λ depends on the profile.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal ridge parameter is universal across variance profiles.

record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: The size-sweep results are presented as curves without tabulated values. The analysis assumes independent feature entries and random regression coefficients; the authors note that real MNIST feature entries are correlated and violate the independence assumption.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying reported size- or sample-sweep results were omitted. Other experiments on training risk, degrees of freedom, and ridge-parameter selection do not measure the claim versions recorded here.

untested.parts: Deep networks: only linear least-squares is studied.
The MNIST sample-size sweep (Fig 7a) is shown, but the text never says whether risk rises with n near p=n.
Any single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Label-noise dependence of the peak. Whether peaks vanish under optimally tuned λ: λ* is derived, but risk versus p/n at λ* is not reported.
Re-plotting against an effective number of parameters.
Model classes other than linear regression.

missing.what: Smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the sample covariance versus p/n for several profiles, including the plateau near zero

record.verdict_notes: The p/n sweep holds n=100 fixed, so it is a parameter-count axis in linear regression, relevant to V4 rather than V1. The constant-profile curve reproduces a known closed form (HMRT22). The MNIST sweep cannot inform V3 because the text gives no direction of risk. No values are tabulated; all evidence is from figures and prose.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network test error as model size grows.
The MNIST experiments vary sample size, but the text does not describe whether risk rises near the interpolation threshold.
The study tests high-dimensional linear regression with variance profiles, not other model classes or a universal claim across all classes.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.

The study reports multiple-descent curves for some variance profiles. It does not vary label noise to test a causal noise account, or test whether the peaks disappear under optimally tuned regularization.
Whether measuring complexity by an effective number of parameters turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relation.reason: Its own analytical results and simulations directly examine ridgeless predictive-risk curves as p/n varies.

tranche.reason: The study extends risk analysis to a new setting of independent, non-identically distributed predictors with variance profiles and reports double and multiple descent.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion paraphrase is supported, including the universal optimal ridge parameter and the discrepancy for correlated MNIST features. Figure-only risk values remain qualitative; no numerical risk values were inferred.

statements.correction: Constant and quasi doubly stochastic profiles: predictive risk increases below p/n=1 and decreases above it; λ=0, α=σ=1, n=100. Deterministic equivalents and simulations are reported. Section 1.3 provides code. Supplied header: arXiv:2403.20200v5, 19 May 2026; reviewed SIAM publication status unverified.
statements.problem: The scientific claims and experimental conditions are supported, but the supplied text does not establish that this study has a reviewed SIAM header; its SIAM references concern other papers.

statements.correction: Piecewise constant and block profiles exhibit triple descent; the polynomial profile exhibits quadruple descent. These are ridgeless numerical results compared with deterministic equivalents. Section 4 describes broad near-zero spectral plateaus and proposes a possible connection to additional descents; an analytical explanation for arbitrary profiles remains difficult. Section 1.3 provides code; reviewed publication status unverified.
statements.problem: Triple and quadruple descent are supported. Separate structural thresholds are not established for this study, and its reviewed publication status is not verified by the supplied text.
